notes: Original system written for this project. It does not follow any published card-picture table (no person-by-initials tables, no table of famous people), and the images were chosen fresh. Not tested with players yet. Every image is common, easy to picture and safe (no brands, no real people). Players are told to make their own pictures, since a picture you choose sticks better than one you are handed. Fact-check (Nov 2, 2026): all 52 images are plain objects and roles; no brand, real person or copied table found. The rule is our own.

rule.name: World and Count
rule.threeSentences: The suit picks a world: Spades is the sea, Hearts is the kitchen, Diamonds is the market and Clubs is the forest. The rank picks the picture: an Ace is one big thing from that world, a number card shows that many of something (two oars, five arms, ten fish), and Jack, Queen and King are always people of that world, the young helper, the expert and the chief. Learn one world and you already know a quarter of the deck.
rule.whyItWorks: Four worlds give you the suit at a glance, and the count hook gives you the rank. You rebuild a picture from the rule instead of memorising 52 loose images.
learningPlan: Day 1: learn the Spades world (13 pictures). Say each card code and its picture aloud, then cover the list and test yourself.
Day 2: Hearts. Day 3: Diamonds. Day 4: Clubs. Take a day off whenever a world still feels wobbly.
Then shuffle and flip single cards, saying the picture within two seconds. Only start Deck Run once you can do that for most of the deck.

makeYourOwn: These are suggestions. If a picture does not work for you, swap it for one that does, and keep the same rule so you can rebuild it. A picture you chose yourself is stronger than one you were handed. The game does not save your own card pictures in 1.1; keep them on paper.
cardCodes: Card code is rank then suit letter: AS is Ace of Spades, 10H is Ten of Hearts, KC is King of Clubs. S is Spades, H is Hearts, D is Diamonds, C is Clubs. Suits are never shown by colour alone (the Cards drill draws each suit as shape and letter).

deckRunGuide.title: How to lay a deck along a route
steps: Pick a route you know well with 13 to 26 stops (a palace, a street or a commute). You need half as many stops as cards, because each stop holds two cards.
Flip the cards two at a time. Turn both into pictures from your card list. Let the first picture do something to the second at the stop, such as pushing, pouring, eating or weighing it.
Move to the next stop for the next two cards. Keep the action short and a little silly. Do not stop to fix a picture that is a bit weak.
At recall, walk the route from stop 1, say the two cards at each stop and place them in order. If a stop is blank, leave a gap and keep going rather than guess.
Check against the deck. Look for the pattern of your errors (a mixed-up suit, a swapped pair) and fix that, not everything.

stops.scene: A big maple leaf with five points is weighed on a two-pan scale, and the scale tips right over the doormat.
Nine pearls spill from an oyster onto a four-legged kitchen table that is reflected in the mirror.

deckRunGuide.honestNote: Memorising the order of a shuffled deck is a memory sport. It trains turning a card into a picture and placing pictures along a route, and it does not carry much into daily life. Cards in Mnemos give no skill points and no Lumen. They are here for people who want the challenge, and you can skip them with no cost to your year.
